newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Pallada Asset Management Fund opens.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Pallada Asset Management Fund opens.

text.p: Pallada Asset Management launched a unit investment fund specialising in GKO discount Treasury bills on Tuesday and plans to launch two more funds in the near future, a top fund official said.

Units in the Pallada Government Securities Unit Investment Fund, one of the first three to be authorised in Russia, will cost 10,000 roubles ($1.82) each with a minimum investment of 500,000 roubles, Pallada chief executive Beth Hebert told a news conference.
Unit investment funds are similar to unit trusts in Britain or mutual funds in the U.S.
Pallada Asset Management was set up by Commonwealth Property Investors, an affiliate of U.S. pension fund adviser, Aldrich, Eastman & Waltch, and Boston Capital Management Group.
Moscow power utility AO Mosenergo is one of the sponsors.
The fund's capital is 1.02 billion roubles.
The company will take no load, or sales fees, during the initial offer lasting three months, said Hebert, a former fund manager for Flemings in Russia.
During this period the company hopes to accumulate not less than 2.5 billion roubles, she said.
The fund is targeted mainly at Russians, but has also prepared sales literature for foreigners. However, it is necessary to purchase units in person in Moscow.
Hebert said the company saw most difficulties in persuading Russians scared by pyramid savings schemes, such as the notorious MMM, to trust their savings estimated at some $20 billion, to the fund.
"We want to win investors' trust, which will provide for long-term development of our funds," she said. "One of the reasons we started a GKO fund is to rebuild investor confidence."
GKOs are the safest and most liquid instrument in Russia.
Pallada Asset Management also plans to open a second fund to concentrate on shares and a third one to invest in real estate, Hebert said.
The Pallada fund is one of the three funds so far approved by Russia's main securities watchdog, the Federal Commission for the Capital Markets.

The other two are The Pioneer First Fund, managed by KUIF, part of the First Voucher Fund (Pervy Vaucherny Fond in Russian), in which Pioneer Group acquired 51 percent last year, and The Credis Fund for Short-Term Rouble Investment, managed by Credis (Moscow), part of the Credit Suisse group.
